1.title: Prompt Engineering and Output Handling
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Prompt Engineering and Output Handling. This module covers the skills prompt engineering, output handling. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Prompt engineering: clear instructions, few-shot examples, system versus user placement, output constraints, iterative refinement. Input sanitization and where instructions live across the prompt. Output handling: structured output, response validation, defensive parsing, and skepticism toward confident output.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's Vague Summaries
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater's Vague Summaries. The prompt says: "Summarize the claim.". Adjusters get summaries of random length and detail, sometimes missing the loss date or the claimed amount. The team wants consistent, useful summaries.

1.title: Prompt Engineering
1.text: Prompt Engineering. Instruction clarity. What to do: Be specific and direct: task, audience, length, what to include, what to omit. Claims example: "Write a five-line summary for an adjuster: loss date, cause, claimed amount, coverage status, open questions". Give context. What to do: Explain the purpose and the audience. Claims example: "Adjusters decide within two minutes whether to escalate". Examples (few-shot). What to do: Show two to five diverse examples of input and output, including edge cases. Claims example: One example with missing data showing "Not stated".

1.title: Prompt Engineering, continued
1.text: Prompt Engineering, continued. System versus user. What to do: System: stable role, rules, format, tone. User turn: the task and the data for this request. Claims example: Rules in system; the claim text and question in user. Output constraints. What to do: State the format, length, fields, and what to do when unsure. Claims example: "If a field is missing write Not stated; never guess". Structure the prompt. What to do: Use tags or headings to separate instructions, documents and questions. Claims example: less than policy greater than, less than or policy greater than, less than claim greater than, less than or claim greater than. Think before answering. What to do: For hard tasks let the model reason (adaptive thinking or ask for step-by-step reasoning in a separate field). Claims example: Coverage analysis.

1.title: Prompt Engineering, continued
1.text: Prompt Engineering, continued. Iterate. What to do: Change one thing at a time, run the evals, keep what improves the score. Claims example: Compare prompt version three with version four on the test set.

1.title: Prompt Engineering, continued
1.text: Prompt Engineering, continued. The figure shows this: A well-structured prompt: stable role and rules in the system prompt; tagged documents, examples, then the task and output format. Placement across components: put stable instructions in the system prompt, per-request data and the task in the user message, and tool descriptions in the tool definitions. Repeating a critical rule at the end of a long prompt can help.

1.title: Prompt Engineering, continued
1.text: Prompt Engineering, continued. Prompt adjustment is empirical: if the model skips a rule, make it more specific, add an example, or move it; do not just add capital letters. Input sanitization: treat user-supplied text as data. Strip or escape characters that could break your tag structure, limit length, and never let user text change the system rules (Module thirteen). Exam tip: Inconsistent or vague output almost always means the prompt is vague: add specific criteria, a format and examples before reaching for a bigger model.

1.title: Output Handling
1.text: Output Handling. The figure shows this: Output handling: ask for structure, parse defensively, validate, check against the source, and handle failure before the result is used.

1.title: Output Handling, continued
1.text: Output Handling, continued. Structured output. Ask for Jason (Java Script Object Notation) that matches a schema: use structured outputs (output config.format with a Jason schema) or a tool with an input schema (strict mode); this removes syntax errors. Response validation. After parsing, validate types, required fields, ranges, enums and business rules (for example the total equals the sum of line items). Defensive parsing. Never assume the reply is well-formed: wrap parsing in error handling, handle missing or extra fields, empty and refusal responses, and truncation (stop reason: max tokens).

1.title: Output Handling, continued
1.text: Output Handling, continued. Skepticism toward confident output. A fluent, confident answer can be wrong: verify against the source, cite the evidence, and route uncertain or high-impact cases to review. Retry with feedback. If validation fails, call again with the specific error; stop after a few attempts. A schema guarantees shape, not truth: values can still be wrong or invented, so validate meaning and ground answers in the provided documents. Ask the model to quote the source text for key facts so the application can check that the quote exists in the document.

1.title: Output Handling, continued
1.text: Output Handling, continued. Never execute or render model output unsafely (as code, H T M L or a database query) without sanitizing it (Module thirteen). Structured outputs use output config.format with a Jason schema, and tools can set strict: true; check the structured outputs page for supported schema features. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: "The model returned plausible but wrong numbers" to validate against the source and add checks; "the Jason sometimes fails to parse" to structured output with a schema plus defensive parsing. Exam tip: A schema guarantees shape, not truth: validate values against the source and business rules.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Clarity: Specific task, audience, length, fields, what to do when unsure. Examples: two to five diverse few-shot examples with edge cases. Placement: Stable rules in system; request and data in user; tags to separate. Iteration: One change at a time, evals, versions, rollback. Sanitization: User text is data; escape tag-breaking input; limit length. Structured output: output config.format Jason schema or strict tool schema. Validation: Shape ≠ truth: check ranges, business rules, source quotes. Defensive parsing: Handle empty, refusal, truncation, missing fields; retry with the error. Skepticism: Confident ≠ correct; verify and review high-impact cases.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Summaries from the prompt "Summarize the claim" vary in length and miss key fields. What is the best first improvement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Clear, specific instructions with a format and examples fix vague output at low cost.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Where should the stable role and formatting rules of an assistant go? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The system prompt holds stable instructions; the user turn carries the request and data.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A prompt mixes instructions with a pasted claim, and the model sometimes treats text inside the claim as instructions. What helps? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Tagging and an explicit data policy reduce confusion between data and instructions.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which technique best shows a model the exact desired output and edge-case handling? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Few-shot examples demonstrate the exact format and the tricky cases better than long written rules.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A parser sometimes fails because the reply contains extra text around the Jason. What is the most reliable fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Schema-constrained output removes syntax variation; defensive parsing handles the rest.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. The model returns valid Jason where the total does not equal the sum of line items. What does this show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Valid structure can hold wrong values; validate business rules.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. What does skepticism toward confident output mean in practice? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Fluent confidence is not proof; ground and verify.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Select two. Which two belong to defensive parsing? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. Expect malformed or truncated output and validate before use.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two are good prompt iteration practices? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Controlled changes with measurement and versioning make improvement reliable.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: D. Question four: D. Question five: D. Question six: C. Question seven: C. Question eight: A and B. Question nine: B and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
